## Quaker Numbered Months: History and Genealogical Significance

This is a great genealogy topic — Quaker records use this convention extensively, and misreading it is a common dating error.

### The Core Reason: Rejecting Pagan Names

When George Fox founded the Religious Society of Friends in the 1640s–50s in England, early Quakers identified that the standard names for both months and days of the week were rooted in paganism and emperor-worship:

| Named Month | Pagan Origin |
|---|---|
| January | Janus (Roman god of doorways) |
| March | Mars (Roman god of war) |
| May | Maia (Roman goddess) |
| June | Juno (Roman goddess) |
| July | Julius Caesar |
| August | Augustus Caesar |

The days of the week were equally problematic — Sunday (the Sun), Monday (the Moon), Tuesday (Týr), Wednesday (Woden/Odin), Thursday (Thor), Friday (Frigg/Freyja), Saturday (Saturn).

Using these names, Quakers believed, gave ongoing honor to false gods. Their **Testimony of Integrity and Plainness** demanded language stripped of anything idolatrous or dishonest. So they substituted ordinal numbers: **First Month, Second Month ... First Day, Second Day**, etc.

### The Critical Genealogy Complication: Which Month Is "First Month"?

This is where researchers get tripped up. England operated on the **Julian calendar** until the **Calendar Act of 1750** (taking effect 1752), and the legal new year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**, not January 1.

So in Quaker records:

| Period | "First Month" means |
|---|---|
| Pre-1752 (most English/colonial records) | **March** |
| Post-1752 (or meetings that adopted Jan. 1 earlier) | **January** |

A record reading *"born 14th of 10th Month 1710"* in old-style Quaker dating means **December 14, 1710** — not October 14. Getting this wrong shifts events by two months.

### What This Looks Like in Records

Quaker monthly meeting registers — births, deaths, and especially marriages — were meticulously kept and are invaluable genealogical sources. A typical entry reads:

> *"Married the 22nd of the 4th Month 1743 at Nottingham Monthly Meeting..."*

In old style (pre-1752), that is **June 22, 1743**.

### The Broader "Plain Speech" Context

Numbered months were part of a wider system Quakers called **Plain Speech**, which also included:
- Using *thee/thou* instead of *you* for individuals (refusing the honorific plural)
- Refusing to remove hats before social superiors
- Rejecting titles like *Mr., Sir, Your Honor*

All of it served the same testimony: no empty deference to worldly rank or pagan tradition.

### Practical Tip for Researchers

When dating Quaker records, always check:
1. **Is this before or after 1752?** (or the meeting's own transition date)
2. **Is the month number consistent with other known dates** in the entry or family?
3. Many colonial American Quaker meetings (Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Virginia) kept old-style dating well into the 1740s even as civil usage was shifting.

Some researchers annotate these as **O.S.** (Old Style) and **N.S.** (New Style) when transcribing, which is good practice to avoid confusion downstream.

Before England adopted the Gregorian calendar reforms in 1752, the **legal year began on 25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January. That created a grey zone every year from **1 January through 24 March**: the modern world's new year had already turned, but England's legal year had not.

|---|---|---|

- It slots the event correctly into a modern chronological timeline.

> Marriage of [name], **15 February 1750/1 (15 February 1751 N.S.)**

## The date "25 March 1750/1" — what it means and why this one needs extra care

### What double dating normally means

In England before 1752, the legal year began on **25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January. Clerks who wanted to be precise about dates from 1 January through 24 March — which fell in different years depending on whether you counted Old Style (OS, legal) or New Style (NS, modern) — wrote both years separated by a slash. For example:

> **6 January 1745/6** = January 6, 1745 by the English legal year, but January 6, **1746** by modern reckoning.

The rule is simple: the second (later) number is the one you use in your research notes, because it matches the modern calendar year.

---

### Why 25 March is the anomalous case — and why this record needs a closer look

**25 March is specifically where the year turned over.** Under the Old Style calendar, March 25 was New Year's Day — the *first* day of the new year. That means:

- **24 March 1750** (OS) → the last day of the old year → double-dated **1750/1** in NS
- **25 March 1751** (OS) → the *first* day of 1751 → **both systems agree it is 1751**

On 25 March itself, the Old Style year and New Style year are **the same number**. There is no ambiguity to resolve, so a slash on that exact date is **anomalous** — the two years written should be identical, not consecutive.

A slash on "25 March 1750/1" suggests one of a few possibilities:
- The clerk applied the double-dating habit one day too late (a common scribal slip at the turn of the year)
- The register has an unusual local convention for when the year turned
- There is a transcription or copying error in the record

---

### What to do before settling on a year

**Check the surrounding entries in the register.** Look at the entries immediately before and after this one and ask:

1. Where does the clerk first start writing "1751" without a slash? That tells you how *this particular register* handles the year boundary.
2. Are there other late-March dates nearby — 22, 23, 24 March — also written with slashes? That would show a consistent local practice you can follow.
3. Does the entry just before this one say "24 March 1750/1" and the entry just after say "26 March 1751"? If so, this entry is almost certainly meant to be **1751**.

---

### Working recommendation

Do **not** automatically record this as 1751 based on the slash alone. Instead:

- Record the date **exactly as written**: `25 March 1750/1`
- Note the anomaly: *"Double-dated on 25 March, which is the OS New Year — year requires verification from surrounding register entries."*
- Once you've checked the register context, record your interpreted year with a brief explanation, e.g.: *"Interpreted as 25 March 1751 NS, based on surrounding entries in the register."*

That way your notes are transparent about what the record actually says and how you reasoned through it.
